extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in disinformation and fake news
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic summary of fake news: its impacts across countries, common disinformation tactics, and public- and private-sector responses (education, fact‑checking, platform moderation, and laws). Useful for readers seeking an overview of how societies identify and respond to false information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy education in schools
rubrics_metrics.description: "include 'media literacy' as one part of school curriculum for the students. It will be included to develop the critical‑thinking skills needed while using social media. Further, the work of media literacy will also include the skills needed to analyze propaganda and sources, so students can clarify what is fake news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach critical‑thinking about social media, train students to analyze propaganda and source credibility so they can identify and reject fake news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform code of practice & regulatory powers (Australia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Australian Code of Practice on Disinformation and Misinformation commenced on 22 February 2021; it asked digital platforms to develop a voluntary code to address disinformation and assist users of their services to more easily identify the reliability, trustworthiness and source of news content. ACMA oversaw the development and recommended legislation to grant ACMA powers to enforce the code, request transparency reports and conduct investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should implement voluntary codes to help users identify reliable sources; regulators may be given powers to enforce codes, obtain transparency reports, and investigate platform measures — with attendant debate about freedom of speech and enforcement design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑checking and collaborative journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative journalism projects and fact‑checking sites (examples: Aos Fatos in Brazil; Verificado 2018 in Mexico) researched online claims, published joint verifications, produced notes and videos documenting false claims and suspect sites, and tracked instances where fake news went viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize multi‑party fact‑checking efforts (news outlets, universities, civil society), systematically research claims, publish verifications and educational material, and track virality to counter misinformation during elections and crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: In‑app verification tools and user hotlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include a WhatsApp 'lie detector' invented to fight fake news within the app and Verificado.mx setting up a hotline where WhatsApp users could submit messages for verification and debunking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy tools that let users submit suspect messages for verification, and build user-facing features within messaging apps to flag or verify forwarded content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation and removal of coordinated inauthentic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms removed fake accounts and content: e.g., Facebook removed 'dozens' of fake accounts directly linked to Bolsonaro's offices; Twitter and Facebook also removed videos or suspended accounts sharing false health claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and remove networks of fake accounts, suspend or takedown demonstrably false content (including deepfakes), and disrupt coordinated amplification campaigns to reduce spread of disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties for producing rumors or fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions criminalize producing rumors or fake news that affect public order or security (example: Saudi Arabia — producing rumors or fake news 'that would affect the public order or public security' punishable by five years and a fine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal penalties can be imposed for spreading certain false information, but such laws risk overreach and censorship if not carefully defined and implemented with safeguards for free expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad 'fake news' laws restricting reporting (Russia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Russia passed laws to ban websites from spreading what the government considers false information and prohibiting 'fake news' regarding the military (with severe penalties, including up to 15 years imprisonment), and also punished materials insulting the state or officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadly worded 'fake news' statutes empower governments to restrict reporting and can lead to closure or exit of independent media and a chilling effect on journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to misuse of the term 'fake news' as a political attack
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'fake news' has at times been used to cast doubt upon credible negative news; political figures (examples: Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu) have labelled unfavorable or critical reporting as 'fake news' to discredit media rather than to identify actual falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between actual demonstrable falsehoods and the rhetorical use of 'fake news' to attack inconvenient reporting; evaluate claims against evidence rather than labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common disinformation tactics to identify
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics described include fabricated polls attributed to reputable outlets, photoshopped images, encrypted/forwarded messages on WhatsApp, astroturfing, bot networks generating large volumes of posts, deepfaked videos, and fabricated viral events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and look for signs of fabricated polls, manipulated images/videos, suspicious amplification patterns (rapid repetitive posting, many bot accounts), and anonymized forwarded messages as indicators of coordinated disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigations and legal scrutiny of disinformation campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial or official investigations (example: Brazil's Supreme Court investigating a purported disinformation campaign) can be used to examine coordinated attempts to spread falsehoods and lead to orders for account removals or other remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal and investigative mechanisms to uncover organized disinformation networks, while balancing due process and avoiding politicization of inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform responsibility to assist users in gathering data online
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives from Facebook Canada told members of Parliament they felt it was their duty to assist individuals in gathering data online and to help in identifying reliable information sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should provide tools, labeling, and educational resources that help users assess the provenance and credibility of online content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi‑stakeholder election‑period interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (Verificado 2018) show coordinated responses involving at least eighty organisations (media, universities, civil society) producing hundreds of verifications and multimedia debunks during an election to counter disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During elections, convene diverse stakeholders to coordinate verification, public education, hotlines, and rapid debunking to reduce the impact of false narratives on voters.
